summary: Describes how an OSPF router can advertise its local addresses in OSPF Traffic Engineering extensions. Other routers need these addresses to compute traffic-engineered MPLS paths to a router's addresses, but previously only addresses tied to TE links were advertised. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5786 lets an OSPF router advertise local addresses that are not already included in Traffic Engineering link data. Other routers can then use those addresses when computing traffic-engineered paths.

subtitle: Adds OSPF Traffic Engineering advertisements for a router's local IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: OSPF Traffic Engineering advertisements include router IDs and addresses on TE-enabled links, but not all local addresses needed as path destinations.
tldr.mechanism: A new Node Attribute TLV carries IPv4 and IPv6 local-address sub-TLVs in an OSPF TE LSA.
tldr.outcome: Other routers can learn additional local addresses for traffic-engineered path computation. RFC 5786 updates RFC 3630 and was updated by RFC 6827 and RFC 8687.

today: RFC 5786 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010. It updates RFC 3630 and has been updated by RFC 6827 and RFC 8687.

sections.title: Why Routers Advertise Local Addresses
sections.content:
OSPF Traffic Engineering extensions advertise a router ID and local addresses for TE-enabled links. They do not include other local addresses such as loopback or non-TE interface addresses. A remote router therefore may not be able to compute a constrained shortest path to one of those addresses.

The RFC gives an example in which separate VPN and non-VPN traffic use different loopback addresses as BGP next hops. The existing OSPFv2 stub-link and OSPFv3 intra-prefix information is not sufficient to reveal all local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers need a traffic-engineered path to an address that is not attached to a TE-enabled link. This RFC adds a way to advertise those additional local addresses.

sections.title: Why Addresses Use a Node Attribute TLV
sections.content:
One possible design was to advertise a separate TE link for each local address. The RFC rejects this because each entry would carry link information that has no meaning for a local address, such as a TE metric.

Instead, local addresses are carried in a new Node Attribute TLV in the OSPF TE LSA. The TLV represents attributes of the router itself and can contain one or more sub-TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: A local address describes a router, not a separate network link. The RFC therefore carries these addresses in a router-attribute TLV rather than advertising made-up links.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Address Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Node Attribute TLV has type 5 and a variable length. This RFC defines an IPv4 local-address sub-TLV with type 1 and an IPv6 local-address sub-TLV with type 2.

Each IPv4 address is encoded as a one-byte prefix length and a four-byte prefix, with zero bits added as necessary. Each IPv6 address contains an 8-bit prefix length, an 8-bit prefix-options field and an address prefix padded to a multiple of 32-bit words.
sections.plainLanguage: The TLV has separate sub-TLVs for IPv4 and IPv6. Each address is accompanied by its prefix length so a receiver can interpret the address fields.

sections.title: What an OSPF Router Advertises
sections.content:
A router advertises one or more local addresses in its Node Attribute TLV. Addresses already available from TE LSAs, such as the router address and TE interface addresses, SHOULD NOT be repeated. Local configuration determines which other addresses are included; the default MAY be to advertise all loopback addresses.

A router MUST NOT place the Node Attribute TLV in more than one TE LSA, or include multiple copies of it in one LSA. The TLV can contain at most one IPv4 local-address sub-TLV and at most one IPv6 local-address sub-TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The router advertises additional local addresses that cannot already be learned from TE link data. It places the address information in one Node Attribute TLV in one TE LSA.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 5786 says it introduces no security issues beyond those discussed in the OSPF Traffic Engineering extensions for OSPF versions 2 and 3. It defines no separate security mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds address information to existing OSPF TE advertisements and says the existing OSPF TE security considerations still apply.

sections.title: IANA Type Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned type 5 to the Node Attribute TLV in the top-level TE LSA type registry. It also created a sub-TLV registry for Node Attribute TLVs, assigning type 1 to the IPv4 local-address sub-TLV and type 2 to the IPv6 local-address sub-TLV.

The RFC sets assignment policies for other values: 3 through 32767 use Standards Action, 32768 through 32777 are for experimental use, and 32778 through 65535 are not assigned at this time.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA assigns a shared number to the Node Attribute TLV and to its IPv4 and IPv6 address sub-TLVs. The remaining number ranges have defined assignment rules.
